name: Beth Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for myself, so the day starts at the kitchen table with coffee and my phone. I've got an AI assistant that turns my site photos and voice notes into quotes, so by eight I've sent two quotes and I'm in the van. Most of my jobs are house rewires, consumer unit swaps and EV chargers on driveways, maybe three customers a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the problem-solving, like tracing a fault in a 1960s house where someone's wired the garage off the lighting circuit. The hard part is crawling under floorboards in winter, my knees are already complaining at twenty-seven. Money-wise I'm doing well, I charge more than most because I'm quick and tidy, and I've got about a year's costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. So everything I've set up was for nothing much. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using for the boring stuff, because it saves me an hour of quoting every evening. I'd probably post in the sparky group I'm in that it never lived up to the hype but it's a good clipboard. I wouldn't be embarrassed about having used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, nothing changes for me. My work is in people's lofts and under their floors, and the AI only ever helped with the paperwork. The only thing I'd think about is Tomas, because he's a software tester and his whole team was nervous, so a plateau is good news for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep the quoting assistant, and probably add a second van with an apprentice next year, since there's more EV and battery work than I can take. I'd keep about a year's costs in savings and put the rest into the business. That's the plan whether AI fizzles or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit relieved for Tomas. Business as usual feels pretty good right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the second van. What would it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A used van, kitted out, is about the same as eight months of my takings after tax, and an apprentice's wage on top. I've already talked to the college about taking someone in September. It's a risk, but there's a waiting list for chargers in my area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a plateau is good news for Tomas. How worried is he today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas (my partner) has watched two people on his test team not get replaced this year. He jokes about retraining as my mate, carrying the cable drums. In this picture that pressure would ease and we'd stop having that talk every Sunday.

say: I'd post that AI never matched the **hype** but is a good clipboard.
I'd say it still saves her **an hour** of quoting every evening.
think: Her work is **hands-on**, so AI only ever touched her paperwork.
A plateau is **good news** for Tomas, her partner, a software tester.
do: Keep the **quoting assistant** running every evening.
Add a **second van** and a college apprentice from September.
Hold about **a year's costs** in savings and invest the rest.
S0.quote: My work is in people's lofts and under their floors, and the AI only ever helped with the paperwork.
fieldNote: She is already **growing**: a second van is planned whatever happens with AI.
Her household worry sits with **Tomas**, whose testing team is shrinking.
She uses AI daily and sees it as a **tool**, not a threat.

steps.text: Buy a used second van and fit it out for chargers
Take on a college apprentice from September
Keep using the AI quoting assistant every evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically what Tomas thinks is already happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be in a trade, honestly, and I'd say it loudly to any school leaver who'll listen. I'd also post about which AI tools actually work for sole traders, because half the sparkies I know are still doing quotes on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's two things. For my business it's mostly upside, the AI does my booking, ordering and quoting, so I can do more jobs with less admin. But my partner Tomas is a software tester, and his job is exactly the checking and coding on that card. If he loses it our income drops by almost half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let AI run more of the office side, booking customers, ordering parts and chasing invoices, and get that second van on the road. I'd also offer Tomas a real role, doing the scheduling and the website for the business, maybe while he retrains. And I'd keep the savings where they are, maybe top them up, until we know what his job is doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited about work and nervous about home, both at once. It's a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Tomas lost his job, what changes first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the holiday we've been planning to Portugal, that's the first thing. Then we'd look at whether he works with me properly or does something else. We're fine for a year on my income and savings, but I don't want him sitting at home feeling useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Tomas actually do electrical work with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He could train, he's good with his hands and he's careful, which is half of it. He'd be thirty when he qualified, which is fine, plenty of people come to the trade late. But I don't want to be his boss and his partner, that's a lot for one relationship.

I'd post which **AI tools** actually work for sole traders.

steps.text: Hand customer booking, parts ordering and invoice chasing to AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Okay. 2028 is basically next year in business terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say trades have a three-year head start and we should use it, not panic. I'd probably try to organise something with the other sparkies in my area, like a shared training day on installing and fixing whatever these robots turn out to be. I'd be the one posting links at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Tomas's job is gone in 2028, I'm fairly sure of that. Then my hands-on work has until about 2031, and chargers on driveways are a pretty standard job, so a robot could learn it. That's both our incomes in five years, which is scary even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop the second van plan and keep the money liquid. I'd sign up for any robotics or automation course I can find, because I'd rather be the person who installs and repairs robots than the one they replace. Tomas would train with me as an electrician straight away, since the thinking jobs are gone first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit sick. I'm good at moving fast, but this is fast for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas on the night the news broke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got my income and a year saved, so we're not going under this month. Then I'd say, start the electrician course in January, you're coming on the vans. I think he'd be relieved to have a plan, even mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the robot installer. What makes you think that work would exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every robot needs power, charging, and someone to fix it when it breaks in a customer's loft. For a few years, at least, that's skilled work nobody's trained for yet. I'm not sure it lasts forever, but it's the next rung.

I'd organise a **shared training day** with local electricians on robots.

She turns Tomas's job loss into a **shared plan** quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a business plan horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good amount of time for a sensible country to get ready, and I'd want my trade body to be running courses on robots by 2028. I'd post about it, sure, but more with plans than doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still both our jobs eventually, just in a better order. Tomas has until 2031, so he can move gradually, and I've got until about 2034 on the tools. That's long enough to change what my business sells, from wiring houses to setting up and servicing home robots and batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still buy the second van, but I'd use it for battery and smart-home work, the stuff that's growing. I'd do an automation course in the evenings next year. And Tomas would start an electrical course part-time while he keeps his job, so there's no gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy, more than scared. Like I've been given homework I actually want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for, to know when to change the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my supplier starts listing robots alongside chargers, I'll know. And when customers start asking if I can install one, I want to say yes the first time. I'd rather be early and a bit wrong than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back on in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a mortgage. We've been looking at houses, but I wouldn't take a big one when I don't know what my income looks like in 2034. We'd rent another couple of years and keep the cash.

fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **business plan**.

steps.text: Buy the second van for battery and smart-home installs
Take an evening automation course next year
Rent for two more years instead of taking a mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, okay. I'm going to sound quite relaxed about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so stop worrying and start learning. I'd probably post about it as an opportunity for trades, because in ten years someone can build a whole business around installing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I like this one. Tomas has until 2036 and I've got until about 2039, when I'm thirty-nine. That's long enough to build a small firm with two or three people and have it doing robot installs by the time they're good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business as planned, the second van, an apprentice, maybe a third van by 2030. I'd use AI for everything office-side so we're lean. And I'd keep putting money into a pension and some shares, so if the robots win completely I'm not starting from zero at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the version where being early actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the apprentice you take on, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea, if it's her, the girl from the college open day, would be about twenty-seven in 2036, my age now. I'd train her on robots as well as wiring from the start. If I'm honest, she'll be better at it than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep money in shares. Why that and not the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots can do my work by 2039, I want to own a slice of whatever makes them. It's a bit cheeky, but it makes sense. The business is for now, the shares are for later.

I'd post that trades can build **whole businesses** around installing robots.

She could build a **small firm** doing robot installs by then.

Put money into **pension and shares** in robot makers.

S4.quote: If robots can do my work by 2039, I want to own a slice of whatever makes them.
fieldNote: She is the rare person who **prefers** this scenario and sees it as growth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's both of us at once and too little time. What would help is fast, cheap training for electricians on installing and servicing robots, and some help for people like Tomas to retrain into trades without losing a year's wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how couples deal with it. Everyone talks about one person's job, but it's households. If one of you is in an office and one of you is on the tools, your clocks run differently. Busy beats scared, every time.

headlineQuote: If one of you is in an office and one of you is on the tools, your clocks run differently.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old self-employed electrician** doing rewires and EV chargers, with a year's costs saved.
She uses **AI every day** for quotes and plans a second van and an apprentice.
Her main worry is **Tomas, her partner**, a software tester whose job AI hits first.
Faced with AGI, she wants to become the person who **installs and repairs robots**.
She grows calmer as warning time grows, and actually **welcomes** the ten-year version.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both her and Tomas's incomes would be threatened within five years.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast, cheap training** for electricians on robots.
Help for office workers like Tomas to **retrain into trades** without losing wages.
